clips.title: The Eureka moment is a dangerous lie
clips.why: Directly attacks the myth every viewer was raised on — the lone genius with one lightning-strike idea — and gives the reason it does damage: it makes people with good seeds of ideas never start. Genuinely counter-intuitive, saveable, and it ends on a self-deprecating joke ('no one writes math formulas on glass') that lands the clip instead of moralising. Two REPLAYED markers sit on exactly these lines.

clips.title: Something is wrong when I make billions and students can't pay their loans
clips.why: A billionaire saying out loud that the system that made him is broken, and then the sharper cut: nobody gives up on a business because they might not earn enough — they never start because they have no cushion to fail onto. The 'you get successful by being lucky too' line, with the coded counterfactual about not having time to learn to code, is the screenshot line. Three REPLAYED markers and live applause confirm the room felt it.

clips.title: I can't even say his name
clips.why: An undocumented top student who isn't sure the only country he has ever known will let him into college — and his birthday wish is a book on social justice. The turn at the end, where Zuckerberg says he cannot name him because it might put him at risk, converts a nice story into something with real stakes. Emotionally complete, needs nothing earlier: the class at the Boys and Girls Club is explained inside the clip.

clips.text: this well remember when I told you about that class I taught at the Boys and Girls Club one day after class I was talking to my students about going to college and one of my top students raised his hand and said that he wasn't sure he could go to college because he's undocumented Ed he wasn't sure if they'd take him last year I took him out to breakfast for his birthday and I wanted to get him a gift so I asked him what he wanted and he just started talking about struggles that he saw other students in his class facing and finally said you know I'd really just like a book on social justice I was blown away here is a young guy who has every reason to be cynical he wasn't sure if the country he calls home the only one he's known was going to deny him his dream of going to college but he wasn't feeling sorry for himself he wasn't even thinking of himself he has a greater sense of purpose and he's going to bring people along with him it says something about our situation today that I can't even say his name because I don't want to put him at risk but if a high school senior who doesn't know what the future holds for him can do his part to move the world forward then we owe it to the world to do our part too

clips.title: Everyone on my management team quit
clips.why: The inside of a story people only know from the movie: big companies circling to buy Facebook, an advisor telling a 22-year-old he'd regret refusing for the rest of his life, and then the line nobody knows — within a year every single person on the management team was gone. His admission ('I felt alone and worse, it was my fault... I wondered if I was an impostor') is the vulnerability that makes it watchable to the end.
clips.start_words: so I never took the time to explain what it was
clips.end_words: so it's up to all of us to create it so we can all keep moving forward
clips.text: so I never took the time to explain what it was that I hoped we'd build a couple years in some big companies wanted to buy us I didn't want to sell I wanted to see if we could connect more people and we were building the first version of Newsfeed at the time and I thought if we could just launch this it could change how we all learn about the world nearly everyone else wanted to sell without a sense of higher purpose this was their startup dream come true and it tore our company apart after one particularly tense argument one of my close advis told me if I didn't agree to sell the company right now I would regret that decision for the rest of my life relationships were so Fray that within a year or so every single person on our management team was gone that was my hardest time leading Facebook I believed in what we were doing but I felt alone and worse it was my fault I wondered if I was just wrong an impostor a a 22-year-old kid who had no idea how things actually worked now years later I understand that is how things work when there's no sense of higher purpose so it's up to all of us to create it so we can all keep moving forward

clips.title: I'm getting kicked out in 3 days, so we need to go on a date
clips.why: The all-time pickup line, told with the absurd setup intact — facing expulsion, parents driving up to pack, friends throwing a going-away party for a living person — and the perfect landing: the prank website that nearly got him expelled led him to Priscilla, who turned out to be the most important thing he built at Harvard. Funny, human, and extremely sendable.

clips.title: Finding your purpose isn't enough
clips.why: The one idea in the speech that isn't standard commencement fare: he rejects 'find your purpose' and replaces it with 'create a world where everyone has one', anchored by the NASA janitor who said he was helping put a man on the moon. The reframe is what makes it more than a well-told anecdote. Lower confidence because the janitor story is widely known and the surrounding language is close to generic.
clips.start_words: today I want to talk about
clips.end_words: moon purpose is that feeling that you are a part of something bigger than yourself
clips.text: today I want to talk about purpose but I'm not here to give you the standard commencement about finding your purpose we're Millennials we try to do that instinctively instead I'm here to tell you that finding your purpose isn't enough the challenge for our generation is to create a world where everyone has a sense of purpose one of my favorites stories is when JFK went to go visit the NASA Space Center and he saw a janitor holding a broom and he asked him what he was doing and the janitor replied Mr President I'm helping put a man on the moon purpose is that feeling that you are a part of something bigger than yourself that you are needed and that you have something better ahead to work for purpose is what creates true happiness

near_misses.why_not: 'Be prepared to be misunderstood' is solid motivational material but says nothing the viewer hasn't heard; loses to the Eureka passage it precedes.
The universal basic income / new social contract stretch is the policy payoff of the luck argument, but on its own it reads as a platform planks list.
The 50x-spent-on-treatment-vs-cures number is a genuine shock fact but it is buried inside a list of project proposals and never taken anywhere.
The closing blessing he sings to his daughter is lovely but belongs to the room; a cold viewer hears a prayer fragment, not a moment.
'First time I'll actually finish something at Harvard' is a good opening joke but pure comedy-finder territory with no depth behind it.

video_read: This is Mark Zuckerberg's full 2017 Harvard commencement speech: jokes about dropping out, then a long argument that the job of his generation is to create purpose for everyone, told through the Facebook origin story, a case for luck and a social contract, and a closing story about an undocumented student he mentors. The strongest standalone material sits in the middle — the 'Eureka moment is a dangerous lie' passage, the billions-vs-student-loans luck argument, and the story of his entire management team walking out — with the emotional peak near the end.
